posts.title: Body, gait or foot shape: which assessment do you need?
posts.summary: A practical guide to the different questions answered by X60, OneScan and F20.

sections.title: Start with the question
sections.body: Before choosing equipment, decide what your team needs to understand. Body composition, walking pressure and foot shape are related, but they are different measurements. A useful demonstration should show the report and the operator workflow as well as the hardware.

sections.title: Match the measurement to the product
sections.body: X60 brings composition, posture and guided mobility observations into one assessment workflow. OneScan is designed for gait and plantar pressure analysis. F20 captures the 3D morphology of both feet, with measurements and model output for suitable downstream workflows. Compare the required outputs with your service, rather than selecting equipment by appearance alone.

sections.title: Plan what happens after the scan
sections.body: Decide who will interpret the report, how it will be explained and whether it needs to be exported. Consider operator training, available space, data handling and integration with existing systems. Ask for a demonstration using the kind of assessment your team expects to perform, and confirm configuration details before purchase.

posts.title: Make repeat assessments easier to compare
posts.summary: Simple operational habits for more useful follow-up records.

sections.title: Agree a repeatable process
sections.body: A follow-up report is more useful when the assessment process is consistent. Document operator instructions and follow the product guidance. Record relevant conditions and any exceptions that could affect a comparison. A clear process also helps new operators deliver the same service.

sections.title: Review observations in context
sections.body: Do not interpret a single measurement without the person’s history, goals and assessment conditions. Compare the relevant measurements and keep notes about changes in the process. Qualified professionals should decide what the observations mean for their work; a report is a starting point for that discussion.

sections.title: Make the next step clear
sections.body: Explain the measurements in plain language and agree when a follow-up is appropriate. Keep reports and notes in the organisation’s approved storage system, with access appropriate to the information. Confirm consent and data handling procedures before introducing any new assessment workflow.

posts.title: Foot shape and plantar pressure tell different stories
posts.summary: Why 3D foot scanning and gait assessment can complement each other.

sections.title: Geometry describes shape
sections.body: A 3D foot scan records the surface and dimensions of the foot. F20 supports full-foot measurement, left-right comparison and STL output. These outputs can contribute to fitting and design workflows when the receiving tools support the format and measurement definitions.

sections.title: Pressure describes contact
sections.body: OneScan records plantar pressure and gait observations on its sensing platform. Pressure distribution and timing give a different view from a 3D model. They should not be inferred from a photograph or a shape model alone. The assessment protocol and interpretation remain important.

sections.title: Bring the outputs together thoughtfully
sections.body: A practitioner may use both types of information when evaluating footwear or orthotic requirements. Confirm how reports and models will be transferred to the next step, and test compatibility before committing to a workflow. Neither scan output replaces a professional fitting, clinical examination or the judgement needed for individual care.
